title: Roth conversion ladder for early retirement
summary: A multi-year strategy to access Traditional IRA/401(k) funds before age 59½ without the 10% early withdrawal penalty.
detailsHtml:
The mechanics

Roth IRA conversions can be withdrawn penalty-free five years after the conversion (each conversion has its own five-year clock). The strategy: in the first year of early retirement, convert one year's worth of expenses from Traditional to Roth, paying income tax at your now-lower bracket. Five years later, withdraw that converted amount tax- and penalty-free. Repeat annually.

Early retiree, age 50, $40K/year needed: Year 1 (age 50): Convert $40K Traditional → Roth, pay tax Year 6 (age 55): Withdraw the Year 1 conversion ($40K) Year 7 (age 56): Withdraw the Year 2 conversion ... continues until age 59.5 when penalty no longer applies

Bridge capital

The first five years of the ladder require funding from outside sources — a taxable brokerage account, prior Roth contributions (which can be withdrawn anytime), or other accessible funds. This is why early retirees need to build a "bridge" of taxable savings before retiring, not just retirement accounts.

IRMAA cliff awareness (size to Medicare tiers, not federal brackets, from age 63). Once you turn 63, your MAGI feeds the Income-Related Monthly Adjustment Amount calculation for Medicare Part B and Part D premiums two years forward — a conversion in your tax year 2026 affects your 2028 Medicare premiums (42 U.S.C. §1395r(i); SSA POMS HI 01101.020). The 2026 first IRMAA tier begins at approximately $109,000 MAGI single / $218,000 MFJ, with five tiers stepping up to combined Part B + Part D surcharges of roughly $578/month per spouse at the top tier ($500K single / $750K MFJ — Part B surcharge $487/month on the $202.90 standard premium, plus ~$91/month Part D). Each tier is a cliff: $1 over the threshold triggers the full surcharge two years later. For an aggressive "fill the 24% bracket" conversion in the year before Medicare enrollment, the inadvertent surcharge can cost each spouse $2,000–$5,000/year for the year that conversion drives. Practical rule from age 63 onward: size conversions to the IRMAA tier boundary, not to the federal bracket boundary. The 12% federal bracket runs to ~$100,800 MFJ taxable income (2026), well below the $218K MFJ IRMAA first tier — so IRMAA usually does not constrain bracket-fill conversions for couples, but it routinely constrains the larger "fill the 22% or 24% bracket" plays the framework's accumulated decumulation guidance otherwise recommends.
SECURE Act 10-year rule strengthens the conversion case. For deaths after December 31, 2019, most non-spouse beneficiaries of inherited Traditional IRAs must distribute the full account within 10 years (IRC §401(a)(9)(H), added by SECURE Act §401). Under the Treasury final regulations issued July 18, 2024 (Treas. Reg. §1.401(a)(9)-5), if the decedent had already begun RMDs, annual RMDs are also required in years 1–9 — not just a year-10 lump sum as the initial planning assumption held. Eligible designated beneficiaries (surviving spouse, minor child of decedent until age of majority, disabled or chronically ill beneficiaries, beneficiaries not more than 10 years younger than the decedent) retain stretch treatment. The practical effect: pre-tax IRA balances inherited by working-age children typically distribute into the child's peak earning years at 32–37% marginal rates. Converting in the parent's lower brackets (10–24%) instead of leaving the bracket-stacked distribution to the child can save 8–20 percentage points on the tax rate spread, materially strengthening the conversion-ladder case for parents with adult children as beneficiaries.
